title: Cirrhosis: Manage the Complication Before the Score
bottomLine: Cirrhosis care is complication prevention and rapid recognition of decompensation. Ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, renal dysfunction and hepatocellular-carcinoma risk each have distinct management pathways; a MELD or Child score supports prognosis but never replaces treatment of the acute complication.
recognize: New ascites, jaundice, confusion, GI bleeding, edema, infection or renal decline mark decompensation.
Patients with cirrhosis can have serious infection with muted fever or leukocytosis.
differentiate: Volume overload from heart/renal disease can mimic ascites/edema; diagnostic paracentesis clarifies new/worsening ascites when indicated.
Coagulopathy/INR in cirrhosis does not equal simple auto-anticoagulation and should not be interpreted as bleeding risk in isolation.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, mental status, ascites, bleeding, infection, renal function, sodium, alcohol/medications and transplant candidacy/goals.
workup: Use diagnostic paracentesis for new/worsening ascites or clinical deterioration when indicated and evaluate bleeding/infection/AKI promptly.
Maintain HCC and variceal surveillance according to current hepatology pathways.
management: Treat ascites with sodium/diuretic strategies and therapeutic paracentesis when appropriate; treat SBP/variceal bleeding/encephalopathy/AKI through urgent syndrome-specific pathways.
Refer decompensated disease for hepatology/transplant assessment when appropriate.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs, sedatives and nephrotoxic drugs can worsen decompensation; medication review is essential.
Do not correct INR/platelets reflexively before low-risk procedures without procedure-specific indication.
counselling: Teach daily weight/abdominal changes, bleeding/infection/mental-status alarms, medication avoidance and alcohol abstinence support without stigma.
followUp: Close the loop on HCC/variceal surveillance, renal/electrolyte monitoring, nutrition and transplant/hepatology care.
examTrap: Focusing on a prognostic score while missing SBP, bleeding or renal failure that needs immediate treatment.
oneLinePearl: In cirrhosis, treat the decompensation first and use scores to support—not replace—clinical decisions.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association for the Study of the Liver cirrhosis resources

title: Hepatic Encephalopathy: Diagnose Clinically and Find the Precipitant
bottomLine: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis in the right liver-disease context after dangerous mimics are considered. Serum ammonia alone cannot diagnose, stage or exclude it; management requires treating the precipitant and reducing gut nitrogen burden while protecting airway and safety in severe cases.
recognize: Sleep reversal, inattention, disorientation, asterixis and reduced consciousness can occur.
Common precipitants include infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration, AKI, electrolyte disturbance and sedating medications.
differentiate: Stroke, sepsis, hypoglycemia, intoxication/withdrawal and intracranial pathology can mimic encephalopathy.
An elevated ammonia without compatible clinical change is not hepatic encephalopathy.
assessment: Assess ABCs, mental status, glucose, infection/bleeding, bowel pattern, volume/renal status, sodium/potassium and sedative/opioid exposure.
workup: Use cause-directed labs/imaging and do not use routine ammonia levels as the sole diagnostic or response target.
Investigate new severe or focal neurologic findings for alternate causes.
management: Treat the precipitant and use lactulose titrated to clinical/bowel response; add rifaximin for recurrent disease according to hepatology guidance.
Severe obtundation or airway risk requires acute monitored care.
medicationSafety: Over-aggressive lactulose can cause dehydration/electrolyte loss and worsen encephalopathy risk.
Avoid unnecessary benzodiazepines, opioids and other sedatives in vulnerable patients.
counselling: Teach patients/caregivers early cognitive/behaviour changes and medication/bowel-plan adherence.
followUp: Review recurrence triggers, lactulose tolerance, rifaximin need, nutrition and transplant/hepatology follow-up.
examTrap: Ordering serial ammonia levels to decide whether a clinically improving patient still has encephalopathy.
oneLinePearl: Treat the patient and the precipitant—not the ammonia number.

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Diagnose the Syndrome, Grade the Physiology, Find the Cause
bottomLine: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed from a compatible syndrome plus enzymes and/or imaging, then managed according to physiologic severity and etiology. Early supportive care, cause identification and monitoring for organ failure matter more than repeating lipase until it normalizes.
recognize: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea/vomiting is classic but variable.
Gallstones and alcohol are common causes; hypertriglyceridemia, medications and post-procedure disease are important alternatives.
differentiate: Lipase elevation can occur in non-pancreatic illness and does not grade severity.
Cholangitis/ongoing biliary obstruction changes urgency for biliary intervention.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, urine output, volume status, fever, biliary symptoms, alcohol, triglyceride/drug history and pregnancy.
workup: Use lipase plus liver tests, renal/electrolyte/glucose and ultrasound for suspected gallstone disease; reserve CT for diagnostic uncertainty or complications rather than routine early imaging in every case.
management: Provide appropriate analgesia, antiemetics, fluid resuscitation with frequent reassessment and early enteral nutrition as tolerated.
Treat the cause and involve GI/surgery for cholangitis/obstruction or complicated disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid indiscriminate large fluid volumes in heart/renal disease; reassess perfusion and overload.
Antibiotics are not routine for uncomplicated sterile pancreatitis.
counselling: After recovery, address alcohol, gallstone, triglyceride and medication causes to prevent recurrence.
followUp: Ensure definitive gallstone management and metabolic/addiction follow-up where indicated.
examTrap: Repeating lipase daily to decide whether pancreatitis is resolving instead of following clinical/organ function.
oneLinePearl: Lipase helps diagnose pancreatitis; physiology tells you how sick the patient is.
sourceBasis: Canadian acute pancreatitis clinical practice resources

title: Gallbladder Disease: Biliary Colic, Cholecystitis, or Cholangitis?
bottomLine: Gallstone disease ranges from transient biliary colic to inflammatory cholecystitis and infected obstructive cholangitis. Distinguish the syndrome using pain pattern, fever/systemic illness, liver chemistry and ultrasound; cholangitis is a source-control emergency rather than routine outpatient gallstone care.
recognize: Biliary colic is episodic postprandial RUQ/epigastric pain without persistent inflammatory illness.
Cholecystitis causes persistent pain/tenderness and inflammation; cholangitis adds biliary obstruction plus systemic infection.
differentiate: Pancreatitis, hepatitis, ulcer disease, ACS and right-lower-lung disease can mimic RUQ/epigastric pain.
Incidental asymptomatic gallstones do not automatically require urgent surgery.
assessment: Assess pain duration, fever, jaundice, vomiting, pregnancy, hemodynamics and comorbidity.
workup: Use RUQ ultrasound as first-line imaging for most suspected gallbladder disease and liver/pancreatic labs to identify obstruction/pancreatitis.
Use advanced biliary imaging when ductal disease remains likely after initial evaluation.
management: Provide analgesia/antiemetics and surgical referral for symptomatic gallstone/cholecystitis pathways.
Suspected cholangitis requires urgent antibiotics and biliary decompression/source-control planning.
medicationSafety: Avoid delaying source control by repeatedly treating presumed biliary infection with antibiotics alone.
Pregnancy changes imaging/medication/procedural planning but does not remove emergency indications.
counselling: Explain why recurrent biliary colic often needs definitive surgical evaluation even if pain resolves between attacks.
followUp: Close the loop on surgical/biliary referral and unresolved liver-test or ductal abnormalities.
examTrap: Treating fever, jaundice and RUQ pain as simple biliary colic and arranging routine follow-up.
oneLinePearl: Gallstone pain can wait; infected obstruction cannot.

title: Colorectal Cancer Screening: Average-Risk Screening Ends When Symptoms Begin
bottomLine: Colorectal screening is for asymptomatic people using the current provincial/territorial program and risk category. Rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, unexplained weight loss or a bowel-pattern alarm requires diagnostic evaluation, not a routine screening FIT and wait.
recognize: Average-risk and increased-risk pathways differ by family history, prior polyps/cancer, IBD and hereditary syndromes.
Provincial screening programs can differ in age/interval/test implementation.
differentiate: A positive screening FIT requires diagnostic colonoscopy; repeating FIT to 'confirm' a positive result is not the pathway.
Symptoms are diagnostic indications, not screening eligibility questions.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then age, family history, prior colonoscopy/polyps, IBD, hereditary risk and ability to complete follow-up.
workup: Use the current jurisdictional screening pathway for asymptomatic patients and diagnostic colonoscopy/imaging when symptoms/risk warrant it.
management: Offer evidence-supported screening with shared decision-making and ensure abnormal tests reach diagnostic resolution.
Refer high-risk hereditary/family/IBD patients to the appropriate enhanced surveillance pathway.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/diabetes medication adjustment for colonoscopy follows procedure-specific guidance rather than blanket holds.
Avoid empiric iron treatment as a substitute for evaluating unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in an appropriate adult.
counselling: Explain the difference between screening and diagnostic colonoscopy and why a positive stool test requires follow-up.
followUp: Track every positive screen to completed colonoscopy/pathology and document the next surveillance interval.
examTrap: Ordering routine FIT for a patient with iron-deficiency anemia instead of initiating diagnostic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms means screening; alarm symptoms mean diagnosis.

title: Colon Polyps: Surveillance Follows Histology, Size, Number, and Exam Quality
bottomLine: Post-polypectomy surveillance is not one universal interval. The next colonoscopy depends on pathology, size/number, completeness of removal, bowel preparation and baseline exam quality; the NP must obtain the actual colonoscopy/pathology report before assigning follow-up.
recognize: Advanced adenoma, multiple lesions, serrated lesions and incomplete/uncertain resection can shorten surveillance.
A low-risk finding after a high-quality complete exam may permit a longer interval.
differentiate: Post-polypectomy surveillance differs from average-risk stool-test screening.
Family/hereditary syndromes and IBD surveillance follow separate pathways.
assessment: Obtain the original procedure/pathology details, preparation quality, resection completeness, family history and prior polyp history.
workup: Do not guess the interval from the patient's memory of 'a polyp'; retrieve the report and apply the current Canadian/provincial surveillance guideline.
management: Schedule the next colonoscopy at the evidence-based interval and ensure unresolved pathology or incomplete excision receives earlier specialty follow-up.
medicationSafety: Procedure medication holds are individualized to bleeding/thrombotic risk and endoscopy guidance.
counselling: Explain why two people with 'polyps' can appropriately receive different surveillance intervals.
followUp: Document pathology-based interval and assign responsibility for recall.
examTrap: Telling every patient with a prior polyp to repeat colonoscopy in the same fixed number of years.
oneLinePearl: Polyp surveillance belongs to the pathology report, not the word 'polyp'.

title: Chronic Constipation: Identify the Mechanism and the Alarm Feature
bottomLine: Chronic constipation is evaluated through stool pattern, medications, diet, pelvic-floor/outlet symptoms and alarm features. Most uncomplicated cases can be treated stepwise without extensive testing, but new obstruction symptoms, bleeding, anemia or weight loss require diagnostic evaluation rather than simply adding more laxatives.
recognize: Hard/infrequent stool, straining, incomplete evacuation and outlet blockage sensations may reflect different mechanisms.
Opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, dehydration and neurologic/metabolic disease commonly contribute.
differentiate: Slow-transit constipation differs from pelvic-floor dyssynergia and medication-induced disease.
Overflow diarrhea can mask severe fecal loading.
assessment: Assess onset, stool frequency/form, straining, digital manoeuvres, diet/fluid, medications, pregnancy, neurologic symptoms and alarms.
workup: Use limited cause-directed labs and colorectal evaluation when indicated; reserve specialized transit/anorectal testing for refractory or outlet-pattern disease.
management: Use fibre when appropriate, osmotic laxatives and other evidence-based agents stepwise; treat impaction/outlet dysfunction specifically.
Pelvic-floor biofeedback is appropriate for documented dyssynergia.
medicationSafety: Avoid chronic stimulant/laxative misuse and magnesium-containing products in susceptible renal disease without review.
Opioid-induced constipation often requires preventive treatment rather than waiting for severe symptoms.
redFlags: New severe constipation in high-risk patient
counselling: Teach realistic stool goals and medication use; daily bowel movement is not required for health.
followUp: Reassess response and investigate refractory disease instead of indefinitely escalating empiric laxatives.
examTrap: Adding another laxative for new constipation plus iron-deficiency anemia without investigating the cause.
oneLinePearl: Constipation treatment follows mechanism; alarms require explanation.

title: Chronic Diarrhea: Classify the Stool Pattern Before Ordering Everything
bottomLine: Chronic diarrhea should be classified by duration, inflammatory/alarm features and plausible mechanism before broad testing. Medication, infection, celiac disease, IBD, microscopic colitis, malabsorption and functional disease require different workups; blood, weight loss, anemia, nocturnal symptoms or immunocompromise increase urgency.
recognize: Watery, fatty and inflammatory patterns narrow the differential but overlap.
Metformin, magnesium, antibiotics, PPIs and many other medications can cause chronic diarrhea.
differentiate: IBS does not explain objective bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory findings.
C. difficile testing should fit a compatible diarrhea/exposure syndrome rather than colonization screening.
assessment: Assess stool character/frequency, blood/nocturnal symptoms, weight, travel/water/exposure, medications, surgery, immune status, diet and family history.
workup: Use CBC/chemistry, celiac/inflammation/stool testing and colonoscopy/imaging selectively according to the phenotype.
Test for infection when epidemiology/exposure supports it rather than ordering every stool assay chronically.
management: Treat the cause, maintain hydration/nutrition and use symptom agents only when obstruction/toxic/invasive infection is not a concern.
Refer persistent inflammatory/malabsorptive or unexplained disease for GI evaluation.
medicationSafety: Avoid antimotility therapy in severe inflammatory/bloody diarrhea or toxic colitis concern.
Review culprit medications before adding chronic antidiarrheals.
counselling: Explain why the stool pattern/exposure history determines which tests are useful.
followUp: Close the loop on abnormal celiac/inflammatory/stool tests and reassess persistent disease.
examTrap: Calling chronic bloody diarrhea IBS because prior colonoscopy years ago was normal.
oneLinePearl: Chronic diarrhea gets narrower when you classify the pattern before ordering the panel.
sourceBasis: Canadian gastroenterology chronic diarrhea practice resources

title: GI Bleeding: Stabilize the Circulation Before the Hemoglobin Falls
bottomLine: GI bleeding is a hemodynamic problem before it is a hemoglobin problem. Assess shock, ongoing bleeding and airway risk, establish resuscitation/access and localize upper versus lower source while remembering that the initial hemoglobin can be deceptively normal in acute blood loss.
recognize: Hematemesis/melena suggest upper bleeding; hematochezia can be lower or brisk upper bleeding.
Tachycardia, orthostasis/hypotension, syncope and poor perfusion signal severity.
differentiate: Iron-deficiency anemia from occult chronic bleeding differs from acute hemorrhagic shock but both require source evaluation.
Anticoagulation increases bleeding severity but does not identify the lesion.
assessment: Assess ABCs, hemodynamics, mental status, ongoing blood loss, anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs, liver disease, pregnancy and prior GI disease.
workup: Use CBC, chemistry, coagulation/type and screen/crossmatch and endoscopic/imaging pathways according to severity/source.
Trend hemoglobin but never wait for a low value to treat clinically significant acute bleeding.
management: Resuscitate with appropriate IV access/fluids/blood products according to physiology and restrictive transfusion principles in stable patients.
Use urgent endoscopy/interventional/surgical pathways for ongoing/high-risk bleeding and treat variceal bleeding specifically when suspected.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic reversal/holding must balance bleeding severity against thrombosis indication and use current protocol.
Avoid unnecessary transfusion in stable patients while never delaying blood for hemorrhagic shock.
counselling: After stabilization, review NSAID/antithrombotic causes and why source evaluation is still needed even when bleeding stops.
followUp: Close the loop on endoscopic pathology, H. pylori, iron replacement and antithrombotic restart plan.
examTrap: Reassuring an actively bleeding hypotensive patient because the first hemoglobin is still normal.
oneLinePearl: In acute GI bleed, the circulation changes before the CBC catches up.
sourceBasis: Canadian GI bleeding and transfusion stewardship practice
